author: AethirCloud

text:
Batteries, staggered job launches and smoothing electronics all help.

But they treat the symptom.

The cause is that a large number of load changes occur at the same point on the network at the same instant.
author: AethirCloud

text:
It is worse on low-inertia grids.

Spinning turbines store rotational energy that resists frequency change.

Inverter-dominated systems have less of that buffer, so the same ramp produces a bigger excursion with no generator fault anywhere.
author: AethirCloud

text:
The result is voltage sag, frequency oscillation and rate-of-change-of-frequency spikes.

Reliability bodies have issued rare high-severity alerts after equipment failures linked to erratic AI training loads.

This is operational now, not theoretical.
author: AethirCloud

text:
A training cluster is one machine.

When thousands of GPUs finish a phase together, a campus can drop 300MW in moments and ramp straight back.

Grids weren’t designed for a customer that behaves like a fault on a schedule 🧵 https://t.co/wyoTEaaXgv
